subject: Economics
description: Annual Financial Statement, types of expenditure, deficit terms, key reforms

questions.stem: Article 112 of the Constitution refers to:

options.option_text: Powers of the Election Commission
Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget)
Citizenship rules of India here
President's emergency powers only

questions.explanation: Article 112 — Pres shall cause to be laid before Parliament the ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT (= UNION BUDGET) of estimated receipts + expenditure for the financial year. STATEMENT shows receipts + expenditure separately for: (a) CONSOLIDATED FUND OF INDIA (most receipts + spending — needs vote of Parliament for outflows); (b) PUBLIC ACCOUNT (PF, deposits — withdrawals not voted upon, but inflows tracked); (c) CONTINGENCY FUND (President's discretion for unforeseen, ~₹500 crore corpus, replenished later). FINANCIAL YEAR (FY): 1 April to 31 March. FRBM Act, 2003 — fiscal discipline. KELKAR Committee, FRBM Review (NK Singh 2017) — recommended further refinements.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Building new highways + dams here also
Salaries, subsidies, interest payments (recurring)
Buying machinery for new factories here
Investment in PSU equity here also too

questions.explanation: TWO TYPES of govt expenditure: (1) REVENUE expenditure — RECURRING, doesn't create assets; e.g., salaries of civil servants, defence personnel; subsidies (food, fertilizer, fuel); interest on past borrowings; pensions; grants to states (most are revenue); maintenance costs. (2) CAPITAL expenditure — creates assets / reduces liabilities; e.g., infrastructure (highways, railways, bridges, ports); buying machinery; loans to states; investments in PSU equity (shares); repayment of loans. INSIGHT: high revenue exp (esp. interest + subsidies) eats into capital exp room → less infrastructure investment. India's ratio: revenue ~80% + capital ~20% (govt aims to raise capex share — recent budgets have done so). REVENUE DEFICIT = Rev. Exp − Rev. Receipts (= 'living beyond means' — usually bad).
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Total expenditure minus total receipts
Fiscal deficit minus interest payments
Revenue expenditure minus receipts
Capital deficit minus revenue gain

questions.explanation: FOUR DEFICIT MEASURES (each tells different story): (1) FISCAL DEFICIT (FD) = Total Exp − Total Receipts excluding borrowings. (2) REVENUE DEFICIT (RD) = Rev Exp − Rev Receipts. (3) PRIMARY DEFICIT (PD) = FD − INTEREST PAYMENTS — shows the shortfall WITHOUT past-debt servicing burden; clean measure of CURRENT fiscal position. (4) EFFECTIVE REVENUE DEFICIT (ERD) = RD − grants for capital creation (introduced 2011-12). PRIMARY DEFICIT close to ZERO = govt's current spending matches current revenue (only borrowing for interest). NEGATIVE PD = primary surplus (revenue > non-interest spending) — desirable in long run for debt sustainability. India's PD has fluctuated; has worsened post-pandemic.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: 1 January to 31 December (calendar year)
1 April to 31 March (existing convention)
1 July to 30 June (some countries follow)
1 October to 30 September (US-style)

questions.explanation: India FY = 1 APRIL to 31 MARCH. Inherited from BRITISH COLONIAL convention (1867); aligns roughly with rabi crop harvest. Different countries: USA Oct 1-Sep 30 (federal); JAPAN + UK April 1-Mar 31 (same as India); GERMANY + most EU + CHINA + CALENDAR YEAR (Jan-Dec). DEBATE: should India shift to calendar year? Considered occasionally (Shankar Acharya Committee, 2017) — but inertia + rabi alignment + transitional cost have kept status quo. UNION BUDGET — earlier presented LAST WORKING DAY OF FEBRUARY at 5 PM (British colonial timing); from 2017 shifted to 1 February at 11 AM (allows Parliament to pass before April 1 start). Railway budget (separate since 1924) merged with Union Budget from 2017.

questions.stem: Which fund's withdrawals require VOTING by Parliament?

options.option_text: Public Account (PF, deposits etc.)
Consolidated Fund of India
Contingency Fund (President's hand)
Personal accounts of ministers

questions.explanation: THREE GOVT FUNDS (Articles 266, 267): (1) CONSOLIDATED FUND OF INDIA (CFI) — main fund; ALL receipts (taxes, borrowings, loans recovered) go in; ALL spending out NEEDS PARLIAMENT'S APPROVAL via APPROPRIATION + FINANCE Bills. EXCEPTIONS — 'CHARGED' expenditure (NOT voted but discussed): salary of Pres, VP, Speaker, judges, CAG, PSC chairmen; debt charges; emoluments of SC judges; pensions; sums needed to satisfy court judgements/arbitration awards. Also includes the Constitution's protected items. (2) CONTINGENCY FUND (Art 267) — President's discretion for unforeseen expenses; ~₹30,000 crore corpus (raised from ₹500 cr in 2021); replenished from CFI later by Parliament. (3) PUBLIC ACCOUNT (Art 266(2)) — money received in trust (PF, post office savings, judicial deposits, etc.) — withdrawals don't need Parliament approval.

questions.stem: When the Lok Sabha passes the Budget but new fiscal year is starting, an interim measure called VOTE ON ACCOUNT allows govt to:

options.option_text: Decide new tax rates instantly here also too
Spend up to 1/6 of estimates for 2 months till budget passes
Borrow without RBI approval for emergency here
Bypass FRBM deficit limits indefinitely here

questions.explanation: VOTE ON ACCOUNT — provision (Article 116) for govt to draw from CFI to MEET ESSENTIAL EXPENSES (salaries, ongoing programmes) for 2-3 months while full budget is being debated + passed. Usually 1/6 of estimated annual expenditure. Used: (a) when election year + outgoing govt presents only interim budget; (b) emergency. INTERIM BUDGET (or 'Vote on Account Budget') — preceding general election: outgoing govt presents one to manage finances till new govt takes over + presents full budget. Used in Feb 2024 by Modi-1 govt (since LS election in April-May 2024). Interim budget conventionally avoids major policy changes. After elections, Modi-2 presented full budget in July 2024.

questions.stem: First UNION BUDGET of independent India (Nov 1947) was presented by:

options.option_text: Jawaharlal Nehru (he was PM) here
R.K. Shanmukham Chetty (1st Finance Minister)
Morarji Desai (later, more famous FM)
Sardar Patel (Home Minister) here

questions.explanation: R.K. SHANMUKHAM CHETTY — first Finance Minister of independent India (1947-49). Presented FIRST budget on 26 NOVEMBER 1947 (interim, for Aug 15, 1947-March 31, 1948). Resigned 1949 (over differences with Nehru on policy). FOR PYQ: MORARJI DESAI — presented 10 budgets (most by any FM). NIRMALA SITHARAMAN (since 2019) — first FULL-TIME woman FM. Indira Gandhi (briefly held FM portfolio, 1969-70) — first WOMAN to present a budget. Other notable FMs: T.T. Krishnamachari, Yashwant Sinha, Manmohan Singh (1991-96, ushered in liberalisation), P. Chidambaram, Pranab Mukherjee, Arun Jaitley. Manmohan Singh's 1991 budget = LANDMARK (LPG reforms — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation; ended licence-permit raj).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In the Union Budget, proceeds from the government's disinvestment of its equity stake in Public Sector Undertakings are classified under which head?

options.option_text: Revenue receipts, since they are non-tax government income
Capital receipts, as they arise from sale of government assets
Revenue expenditure, since PSU operations are revenue items
External debt receipts under the capital account of balance

questions.explanation: B is correct because disinvestment involves selling government-owned equity (an asset), making it a non-debt capital receipt. Option A is wrong because revenue receipts cover recurring income like taxes and dividends, not proceeds from asset liquidation. Disinvestment does not create a liability for the government, so it falls under non-debt capital receipts specifically.

questions.stem: The Economic Survey — the government's flagship annual review of India's economic performance — is customarily presented before Parliament:

options.option_text: On the same day as the Union Budget, before the Finance Minister's speech
One day before the Union Budget is presented in Lok Sabha
Two weeks before the Budget, to allow adequate deliberation time
On the last working day of the outgoing fiscal year's third quarter

questions.explanation: B is correct: the Economic Survey, prepared by the Chief Economic Adviser, is tabled in Parliament a day before the Union Budget to give legislators the macroeconomic context for the fiscal proposals. Option A is wrong — it is a separate document tabled on a separate day, not during the Budget speech itself.

questions.stem: Expenditure 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India differs from 'voted' expenditure primarily because it:

options.option_text: Requires joint approval from both Houses of Parliament each session
Is not subject to parliamentary vote and is paid as a matter of right
Is sanctioned exclusively for defence and national security purposes
Must first receive clearance from the Public Accounts Committee

questions.explanation: B is correct: charged expenditure (e.g., salaries of the President, Supreme Court judges, CAG, election commissioners) is paid directly from the Consolidated Fund without Parliament's vote — Parliament can only discuss it, not vote it down. Option A is wrong because it is specifically the immunity from voting that defines charged expenditure; no joint session approval is involved.

questions.stem: Under Article 267 of the Constitution, the CONTINGENCY FUND OF INDIA is held at the disposal of which authority, enabling advances for unforeseen expenditure pending Parliament's authorisation?

options.option_text: Parliament, through a resolution passed during a special session
President of India, on the advice of the Council of Ministers
Finance Minister, independently and without prior RBI concurrence
Reserve Bank of India, acting as the government's statutory banker

questions.explanation: B is correct: Article 267 places the Contingency Fund at the disposal of the President (in practice, operated on the advice of the Council of Ministers), allowing urgent advances before Supplementary Demands for Grants can be placed before Parliament. Option C is wrong — the Finance Minister does not operate it independently; it remains constitutionally vested in the President.

questions.stem: The FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY AND BUDGET MANAGEMENT (FRBM) Act, 2003 obligates the Central Government to place before Parliament, along with the Budget, a statement indicating the medium-term fiscal targets. This document is known as the:

options.option_text: Medium Term Fiscal Policy cum Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement
Annual Financial Statement as mandated under Article 112 of Constitution
Macro-Economic Framework Statement for the upcoming financial year
Economic Survey supplementary note tabled by the Finance Ministry

questions.explanation: A is correct: FRBM rules require three statements — the Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement, the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, and the Macro-Economic Framework Statement. These are often jointly referred to as 'MTFP cum FPS Statement'. Option C (Macro-Economic Framework Statement) is also a required FRBM document but is a distinct statement; Option B describes the constitutional budget document, which predates FRBM.

questions.stem: The Union Budget shows a fiscal deficit of ₹17.86 lakh crore and interest payments of ₹11.90 lakh crore for the year. What is the PRIMARY DEFICIT for that year?

options.option_text: ₹29.76 lakh crore — sum of fiscal deficit and interest outgo
₹5.96 lakh crore — fiscal deficit minus the interest payments
₹11.90 lakh crore — interest payments alone define primary deficit
₹17.86 lakh crore — primary deficit equals gross fiscal deficit always

questions.explanation: B is correct: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments = ₹17.86 − ₹11.90 = ₹5.96 lakh crore. Primary deficit strips out the debt-servicing cost to reveal the government's fresh borrowing need for current operations. Option C is a common trap — interest payments are what you subtract to get primary deficit, not the primary deficit itself.

questions.stem: Under Article 266(2) of the Constitution, the PUBLIC ACCOUNT OF INDIA holds moneys received by the government that do NOT form part of the Consolidated Fund. Which category BEST describes the nature of such moneys?

options.option_text: Tax revenues collected directly from corporations and individuals each year
Funds held in fiduciary capacity — e.g., provident funds and small savings deposits
Market borrowings raised via government securities and treasury bills issued
External grants received by the Union from bilateral and multilateral donors

questions.explanation: B is correct: the Public Account holds moneys where the government acts as a banker or trustee — provident funds, small savings, deposits — rather than as owner. Parliament's authorisation is not required for withdrawals because the government has a repayment obligation. Option C (market borrowings) is wrong — those flow into the Consolidated Fund as capital receipts; Option A (tax revenues) also goes into the Consolidated Fund, not the Public Account.
